title: How Analysts Segment Whisky Drinkers | Craft Beer School
desc: How drinks company analysts split whisky drinkers by price tier, occasion, repertoire and need state, plus what each cut can tell you.
teaser: Age and income are the weakest way to split whisky drinkers. Occasion and repertoire tell you far more.
standfirst: Every whisky brand plan starts with a picture of who drinks it. This guide shows the segmentation cuts analysts actually use, what the liquid has to do with each one and where the numbers mislead.
sections: Demographics are the starting point, not the answer

The first cut most teams reach for is age, gender, income and city tier. It is easy to buy and easy to chart. It is also the weakest predictor of what someone pours. Two 35 year old managers in Pune on the same salary can drink completely different whiskies on the same evening.

In India there is a legal floor before any of this starts. The legal drinking age is set by each state and ranges from 18 to 25, so every segment definition, survey screener and media plan has to start above the strictest age that applies to that market. Anyone below it is not a segment. They are out of scope.

Use demographics to size and reach a segment. Use the cuts below to understand it.
Price tier is how the trade already thinks

The Indian whisky business talks in price segments: regular, deluxe, premium and prestige or luxury above that. These tiers line up with what is in the bottle. Most regular and deluxe whisky in India is a blend built on extra neutral alcohol, a highly purified spirit from molasses or grain, with malt spirit, flavour and colour. Premium tiers bring in more malt, bottled-in-India Scotch and Indian single malts. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky explains the categories.

Price tier works as a segment because it is observable in sales data. A depot ships cases by SKU and every SKU sits in one tier. The trap is assuming a drinker lives in one tier. Many trade up for a wedding or a gift and trade down at month end.

Occasion segmentation asks where and why a drink happens instead of who drinks it. Typical whisky occasions are a weekday drink at home, a weekend party with friends, a bar or restaurant visit, a celebration and a gift. Each has its own price expectation, pack size and serve.

The same drinker might choose a 180 ml bottle of a deluxe blend for a quiet Tuesday and a 750 ml premium bottle to carry to a friend's housewarming. Occasion explains that switch. Demographics cannot. In India the serve matters too: whisky with water, soda or ice is the everyday norm, while neat or with a few drops of water is more of an enthusiast occasion.
Repertoire shows how loyal drinkers really are

Very few whisky drinkers buy one brand only. Most hold a repertoire of three or four brands they move between. Analysts measure this as share of repertoire: of the occasions a drinker had in a period, what fraction went to your brand. A brand with many light buyers and few loyal ones behaves very differently in a price increase from a brand with a small, devoted base.

Repertoire data comes from household or consumer panels, loyalty data where retail allows it and surveys that ask which brands were bought in the last month. Each source has gaps. In many Indian states retail is run or licensed by the state, so the till data a grocery analyst takes for granted is often not available.
Need states connect the segment to the liquid

A need state describes what the drinker wants from the glass: something smooth and easy with soda, something to show taste in front of friends, something smoky to explore, something to mark a promotion. Need states matter to us as brewers and distillers because they map onto real liquid choices.

  • Smooth and mixable: lighter blends, low peat, little oak bite, built to stay pleasant when diluted with soda and ice.
  • Discovery: single malts, peated whisky, sherry cask finishes, cask strength bottlings around 55 to 60% ABV.
  • Status: age statements, heavy glass, gift packs.

When a marketing brief asks for a whisky for the discovery drinker, the blender hears a specific profile. When a dashboard shows a need state segment shrinking, the question for the liquid team is whether the product still delivers that profile.

Three things trip up analysts who are new to whisky.

  1. Shipments are not drinking. Primary sales from the company to a distributor or state corporation can move weeks ahead of consumption. A segment that looks like it grew in March may only have been stocked before the financial year closed.
  2. Survey answers flatter. People over-report premium brands and under-report quantity. Weight survey data against sales volumes in 9 litre cases, the trade's standard unit of twelve 750 ml bottles.
  3. States are separate markets. Tax and price rules differ by state, so a premium segment in one state can sit at a regular price point next door. Build segments within a state before you roll them up.
A first segmentation you can build this week

Take one state where your team has clean secondary sales by SKU. Tag every SKU with its price tier and pack size. Then add one occasion field from the pack: 180 ml and 375 ml packs lean towards personal and at-home occasions, 750 ml and gift packs towards sharing and gifting. That single table, read month by month, will already show you trading up and trading down that the national total hides.

If your team also wants to know what the drinker tastes in each tier, a guided, opt-in nosing session is the fastest way to make the price ladder real. Our guide to whisky tasting for beginners is a good place to start.
faqs: What is the most useful way to segment whisky drinkers?
Occasion and repertoire usually explain more than age or income. Use demographics to size and reach a segment, then occasion and need state to understand it.
Why do price tiers matter so much in Indian whisky?
They line up with the liquid and with how sales data is recorded, since every SKU sits in one tier. Many states also tie excise to declared price, so tiers shape pricing too.
Can segmentation include people under the legal drinking age?
No. The legal drinking age is set by each state, so every screener and media plan must start above the strictest age that applies in that market.
